newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's top anti-drug warrior fired for drug links.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's top anti-drug warrior fired for drug links.

text.p: The Mexican government on Tuesday fired its top anti-drug fighter and said it was charging him with drug corruption.

In a major embarrassment for the government of President Ernesto Zedillo, Army Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, head of the National Institute for the Combat of Drugs (INCD), was fired for alleged links to Amado Carrillo Fuentes, the country's most powerful drug baron.

"Today we have a well-founded presumption that he and personnel under his direct command have been and are collaborators of the criminal organisation headed by Amado Carrillo Fuentes," Defence Minister Enrique Cervantes told a news conference.

"The Defence Ministry considers well-founded the presumption that in recent years Gen. Gutierrez deceived his superiors, betrayed the confidence placed in him, damaged Mexico's national security and harmed joint institutional efforts against drug-trafficking," he added.
"It is a very painful thing for those of us who love Mexico."

Rebollo, 62, was appointed to his job only two months ago. He disappeared from public view last week and officials said on Monday that he was in a military hospital after suffering a heart attack on Feb. 7.
Cervantes said on Tuesday his health problems came on precisely when he confronted Gutierrez in his office with evidence of his suspected corruption 11 days ago.
"The arrest warrant against Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo could be carried out at any moment," Attorney General Jorge Madrazo Cuellar told the news conference.
Cervantes listed nine points on which the charges against Gutierrez were based.

The most serious appeared to be that he had moved into a luxury apartment well beyond his means upon starting his new job in Mexico City, and that the apartment was made available to him by a suspected Carrillo lieutenant.
The same man, Eduardo Gonzalez Quirarte, allegedly gave "considerable sums of dollars in cash" and encrypted communications devices to people working directly with Gutierrez.
The scandal was also likely to embarrass the United States, which had praised Gutierrez highly for his record of arrests of major drug-traffickers.

Cervantes said that while Gutierrez was very effective against some drug gangs, he was protecting Carrillo's Juarez Cartel, described by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration as Mexico's most powerful.
Zedillo, in a statement, said the charges against Gutierrez showed that "no one can be above the law ... justice cannot be selective."
The newspaper Siglo 21 reported on Tuesday that over the weekend the military launched a surprise raid on three of Gutierrez's homes in the western city of Guadalajara and arrested four people.
One local reporter who knew the general well said the Gutierrez affair might not be all it seemed.

The reporter, who asked not to be identified, said he understood from local police sources that the operation might have been an attempt by corrupt generals to topple Gutierrez because of his proven efficiency in hitting drug cartels.
"We think this could be a personal vendetta against the general ... by army members who are protecting drug traffickers," he said.

The confusion surrounding the general was the second drug scandal to erupt in Mexico this week. Over the weekend, two Mexican newspapers published what they said was testimony from witnesses in the United States who alleged that then-President Carlos Salinas de Gortari and his family had partied with a top drug trafficker and benefited from drug money.
Salinas and his jailed brother Raul denied the allegations through their lawyers.
